units.title: Unit 1: Early River Valley Civilizations (Mesopotamia & Egypt)

lessons.title: Mesopotamia & Ancient Egypt (Part 1 of 1)
lessons.reading: Rivers provided fresh water and rich silt for farming surpluses. Mesopotamia grew between the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers (developing cuneiform and Hammurabi’s Code), while Egypt flourished along the Nile River.

principles.title: Mesopotamia, Ancient Egypt & River Valley Geography
principles.summary: Explain how river valleys supported surpluses, writing systems, and written laws.

bank.prompt: Why did early civilizations begin along major river valleys?
choices: Rivers gave fresh water and fertile soil for farming
River valleys had no weather or seasons
Mountains blocked all rain from falling
Rivers were made of salt water
bank.answer: Rivers gave fresh water and fertile soil for farming
bank.explanation: Seasonal river floods left rich silt that helped farmers grow food surpluses.

bank.prompt: Mesopotamia developed between which two rivers?
bank.answer: Tigris and Euphrates Rivers
bank.explanation: Mesopotamia means "land between the rivers" and lay between the Tigris and Euphrates.

bank.prompt: Why was the Code of Hammurabi historically important?
choices: It was an early written law code displayed in public
It was the first map of the Pacific Ocean
It ended all farming in Babylon
bank.answer: It was an early written law code displayed in public
bank.explanation: Hammurabi’s Code was carved in stone so citizens could see written laws and punishments.

bank.prompt: What wedge-shaped writing system did Sumerians invent?
bank.answer: Cuneiform
bank.explanation: Cuneiform is the wedge-shaped writing Sumerians pressed into wet clay tablets.

bank.prompt: How did farm surpluses lead to job specialization?
choices: Extra food let some people become artisans and scribes
Everyone had to hunt wild herds all day
Kings banned people from making pottery
bank.answer: Extra food let some people become artisans and scribes
bank.explanation: A food surplus meant not everyone had to farm, so workers could specialize in crafts and trade.

bank.prompt: Which artifact helped scholars translate Egyptian hieroglyphics?
bank.answer: The Rosetta Stone
bank.explanation: The Rosetta Stone had the same message in Greek and hieroglyphics, unlocking the translation.

bank.prompt: Why was Egypt called "the Gift of the Nile"?
choices: Nile floods brought water and rich soil
The Nile River flowed uphill into mountains
Greece gave the river to Egypt
The Nile froze solid every summer
bank.answer: Nile floods brought water and rich soil
bank.explanation: Without the Nile’s predictable floods and fertile silt, Egypt would have been barren desert.

bank.prompt: What were stepped pyramid temples in Mesopotamia called?
bank.answer: Ziggurats
bank.explanation: A ziggurat was a terraced mud-brick temple tower built at the center of a Mesopotamian city.

units.title: Unit 2: Classical Greece & Rome, World Religions & Silk Road Trade

lessons.title: Athenian Democracy & The Roman Republic (Part 1 of 2)
lessons.videoTitle: Khan Academy: Classical Greece and Rome
lessons.reading: Mountains divided Greece into city-states like Athens, which created direct democracy. Rome built a republic where citizens elected representatives and posted laws on the Twelve Tables.

principles.title: Athenian Direct Democracy vs. Roman Representative Republic
principles.summary: Compare Greek direct democracy, Roman republican government, and primary sources.

bank.prompt: How did mountains shape ancient Greek government?
choices: Flat plains united Greece into one kingdom early on
Lack of seas stopped all Greek boat travel
Thick ice covered every Greek island
bank.answer: Isolated valleys formed independent city-states
bank.explanation: Mountain barriers separated Greek communities into independent city-states called poleis.

bank.prompt: How does direct democracy differ from a republic?
choices: Citizens vote on laws directly instead of electing representatives
A king makes every law without any vote
No citizen is allowed to speak in public
Generals rule the country by force
bank.answer: Citizens vote on laws directly instead of electing representatives
bank.explanation: In direct democracy (Athens), citizens vote on laws themselves; in a republic (Rome), they elect representatives.

bank.prompt: What was the main purpose of Roman aqueducts?
choices: Carrying fresh water from hills into cities
bank.answer: Carrying fresh water from hills into cities
bank.explanation: Aqueducts were stone channels and bridges that used gravity to bring fresh water to Roman cities.

bank.prompt: What was Rome’s first written law code called?
bank.answer: The Twelve Tables
bank.explanation: The Twelve Tables were bronze tablets posted in the Roman Forum listing citizens’ legal rights.

bank.prompt: Which item is a primary source from ancient Rome?
choices: A silver coin minted under Emperor Augustus
A 2024 history textbook chapter on Rome
An online encyclopedia article written today
bank.answer: A silver coin minted under Emperor Augustus
bank.explanation: A primary source is an original object or document created during the time period being studied.

bank.prompt: What is a modern biography of Julius Caesar classified as?
bank.answer: A secondary source
bank.explanation: A secondary source is created long after an event by someone who did not witness it firsthand.

bank.prompt: Which Greek philosopher taught by asking probing questions?
bank.answer: Socrates
bank.explanation: Socrates developed the Socratic Method, using careful questions to test ideas and logic.

bank.prompt: Why did the Roman Republic divide power into three branches?
choices: To create checks and balances so no one ruled alone
To make sure only one king held all power
To stop citizens from ever voting
bank.answer: To create checks and balances so no one ruled alone
bank.explanation: Dividing power among Consuls, the Senate, and Assemblies prevented any one leader from becoming a tyrant.

lessons.title: Ohio Eastern Hemisphere: Religions, Silk Road & Trade (Part 2 of 2)
lessons.videoTitle: Khan Academy: The Silk Road & Cultural Diffusion (OH.6.SS.7 / OH.6.SS.13)
lessons.reading: Along the Silk Road, merchants traded silk and spices while spreading technologies and world religions like Buddhism (cultural diffusion). Regions specialize in goods based on local resources, supply, demand, and opportunity cost.

principles.title: Eastern Hemisphere Religions, Cultural Diffusion & Trade Economics
principles.summary: Explain Silk Road cultural diffusion, world religions, scarcity, and opportunity cost.

bank.prompt: What was the Silk Road across the Eastern Hemisphere?
choices: A network of trade routes linking China and the Mediterranean
A single highway paved with silk cloth
A sea route around South America
A stone wall built across Greece
bank.answer: A network of trade routes linking China and the Mediterranean
bank.explanation: The Silk Road was an overland web of caravan routes connecting China, Central Asia, India, and Rome.

bank.prompt: What does cultural diffusion mean in world history?
choices: The spread of ideas, religions, and technology between cultures
Keeping every invention hidden inside one city
Building tall walls to stop all trade
bank.answer: The spread of ideas, religions, and technology between cultures
bank.explanation: Cultural diffusion is the exchange of beliefs, customs, and inventions when different societies trade and meet.

bank.prompt: Which world religion spread from India to China along the Silk Road?
bank.answer: Buddhism
bank.explanation: Monks and merchants traveling the Silk Road carried Buddhism from India into Central Asia and China.

bank.prompt: Why do countries specialize in making certain goods to trade?
choices: Resources are unevenly distributed across regions
Every country has the exact same climate and soil
Trade makes goods more expensive for everyone
No country ever needs food or fuel
bank.answer: Resources are unevenly distributed across regions
bank.explanation: Regions specialize in goods suited to their local resources and trade for items they cannot easily produce.

bank.prompt: In economics, what happens when a popular good becomes scarce?
choices: Stores give it away for free
bank.answer: Its price tends to rise
bank.explanation: Scarcity means limited supply. When demand is high and supply is low, prices rise.

bank.prompt: What is opportunity cost when making an economic choice?
choices: The value of the next-best choice you give up
The sales tax printed on a receipt
The weight of gold coins in a bank
A free gift given at a market
bank.answer: The value of the next-best choice you give up
bank.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative you give up when you choose one option over another.

bank.prompt: How did most goods travel across the 4,000-mile Silk Road?
choices: In stages through relay trade between oasis cities
By steam train in a single day
By cargo airplanes over the mountains
One merchant walked the whole way alone
bank.answer: In stages through relay trade between oasis cities
bank.explanation: Merchants traded goods from one oasis trading post to the next in a relay system.

bank.prompt: Which three major monotheistic religions began in Southwest Asia?
bank.answer: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam
bank.explanation: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam all originated in Southwest Asia and teach belief in one God (monotheism).
